summary: Describes how to use TLS with mutual X.509 authentication to secure NETCONF. It is a revision of RFC 5539 and documents operational experience.

eli5.summary: Both sides show ID cards before the secret conversation about device settings begins.

questions: what port does netconf over tls use
how does netconf derive a username from a certificate
subtitle: How NETCONF device-management sessions run over TLS, with both sides proving who they are using X.509 certificates.

tldr.problem: NETCONF manages the configuration of network devices, so its connection must be private and both ends must be sure who they are talking to.
tldr.mechanism: The NETCONF client acts as the TLS client and connects to TCP port 6513. Both peers present X.509 certificates, and the server maps the client's certificate to a NETCONF username before the session starts.
tldr.outcome: This revision of RFC 5539 adds the NETCONF 1.1 message framing and a described way to derive usernames from certificates. It has since been updated by RFC 9918.

today: RFC 7589 is a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 5539, and it has been updated by RFC 9918. Read the two together for the current rules.

sections.title: Why NETCONF Needs TLS
sections.content:
NETCONF, defined in RFC 6241, is a way to manage a network device. It needs a persistent connection that provides integrity, confidentiality, peer authentication and reliable, sequenced delivery. This document says how to carry NETCONF messages over Transport Layer Security (TLS), specifically TLS as defined in RFC 5246.

Implementations MUST support mutual, certificate-based TLS authentication. That assures the server of the identity of the principal who wants to change the management information, and assures the client of the identity of the server it wants to manage.
sections.eli5: Changing a router's settings is a big deal, so both sides must be sure they are talking to the right one. Each side shows an ID card first.

sections.title: Opening and Closing the Connection
sections.content:
The peer acting as the NETCONF client MUST act as the TLS client. It opens the connection, and the server passively listens on the well-known TCP port 6513. The client sends the TLS ClientHello to begin the handshake, and the server MUST send a CertificateRequest so that the client has to present a certificate.

Identity verification of both sides is finished before the NETCONF <hello> message is sent, so verification is completed before the NETCONF session starts.

The session ends with the <close-session> operation. When the server processes it, the server SHALL respond and close the TLS session as described in Section 7.2.1 of RFC 5246.
sections.eli5: The visitor knocks on door number 6513 and the house asks for an ID card. Only after the ID checks do they start the real conversation, and they say goodbye properly at the end.

sections.title: Message Framing
sections.content:
All NETCONF messages MUST be sent as TLS application data. One TLS record can hold several NETCONF messages, and one message can be split across several records, so NETCONF needs its own way to mark where a message ends.

The earlier version, RFC 5539, used the framing from RFC 4742. This version follows RFC 6242. The <hello> message MUST be followed by the character sequence ]]>]]>. After each side reads the other's hello and sees its capabilities, there are two cases:

  • If both peers advertise the :base:1.1 capability, the chunked framing from Section 4.2 of RFC 6242 is used for the rest of the session.
  • Otherwise the older end-of-message mechanism from Section 4.3 of RFC 6242 is used.
sections.eli5: Messages arrive like a long ribbon, so you need a marker to show where one note stops. The first note ends with a special stamp, and newer partners then switch to a better way of labelling each piece.

sections.title: Checking Certificates and Identities
sections.content:
Both peers MUST use X.509 certificate path validation (RFC 5280) on the certificate the other side presents. A certificate can also be accepted if it matches one obtained by another trusted mechanism, such as a locally configured certificate fingerprint. If path validation fails and no such match exists, the connection MUST be terminated as defined in RFC 5246.

The client MUST check the identity of the server according to Section 6 of RFC 6125. The server MUST verify the identity of the client before the NETCONF session starts.
sections.eli5: Each side checks that the other's ID card was issued by someone trustworthy, or that it matches a card they already know. If the card looks fake, the door slams shut.

sections.title: From Certificate to NETCONF Username
sections.content:
NETCONF requires the transport's authentication to produce an authenticated client identity, commonly called the NETCONF username, whose permissions the server knows. The RFC describes an algorithm, the same one used in the SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB and in the ietf-x509-cert-to-name YANG module.

The server keeps an ordered list of mappings. Each entry has a certificate fingerprint, a map type, and optional auxiliary data. The server walks the list in order. An entry matches if its fingerprint equals the presented certificate's fingerprint, or equals that of a locally held trusted CA certificate that is part of the certificate's CA chain.

The map type then says how to get the username:

  • specified: the username is explicitly configured in the auxiliary data.
  • san-rfc822-name, san-dns-name, san-ip-address: taken from the matching subjectAltName field, with lowercase conversion rules for names and IP address formatting rules.
  • san-any: the first matching subjectAltName value of those types.
  • common-name: the certificate's CommonName converted to UTF-8. Its use is deprecated in favor of subjectAltName methods.

If no username can be determined from an entry, or the result does not comply with NETCONF's username requirements, the server MUST keep searching later entries. If none remain, the TLS session MUST be terminated. The username is passed to the NETCONF layer without modification.
sections.eli5: The guard has a list. He finds the page that matches your ID card, and that page tells him what name to call you. If no page fits, you are not let in.

sections.title: Cipher Suites
sections.content: Implementations MUST support TLS 1.2 and are REQUIRED to support the mandatory-to-implement cipher suite. They MAY implement additional cipher suites that provide mutual authentication and the confidentiality NETCONF needs, and they SHOULD follow the recommendations in RFC 7525.
sections.eli5: Everyone must at least know one common secret code. They may learn more codes, as long as those keep the conversation private and prove who is who.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
NETCONF reads and changes configuration and state, which may include sensitive data such as usernames or security keys, so access must be limited to authorized users and systems. The security considerations of TLS and NETCONF also apply.

If a deployment trusts a white-listed CA certificate for clients, that CA should be used only to issue certificates for accessing NETCONF servers. Otherwise every certificate it issues for other purposes would be accepted by a NETCONF server too, which is likely not suitable.

Third-party authentication, such as a backend AAA server, is not supported, because TLS does not specify it and NETCONF depends on the transport for authentication. Where it is needed, the SSH transport of RFC 6242 can be used.

RFC 5539 wrongly assumed that the end-of-message sequence ]]>]]> cannot appear in a well-formed XML document. Sent deliberately, it can cause operational problems and open the door to attacks, although the threat is believed not to be very high. This document still uses it for the initial hello for compatibility, and uses chunked framing afterwards when both peers support :base:1.1, to avoid injection attacks.
sections.eli5: Do not hand out a master key. If one office issues ID cards for many buildings, anyone with such a card could walk into the NETCONF building too.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 5539
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the changes from RFC 5539:

  • Documented that the new message framing is used when both peers support the :base:1.1 capability.
  • Removed text that duplicates the TLS and NETCONF specifications, restructured the text, and aligned with RFC 6125.
  • Added a high-level description of how NETCONF usernames are derived from certificates.
  • Removed the reference to BEEP.

IANA's registration of TCP port 6513 with the service name netconf-tls was made under RFC 5539, and this document restates the registration template with itself as the reference.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition of the rulebook. It adds a better way to mark where messages end and explains how the guard picks your name.

messages.label: ClientHello
messages.note: Opens the TLS handshake to TCP port 6513.

messages.label: CertificateRequest
messages.note: The server MUST ask for a client certificate.

messages.label: close-session
messages.note: The server responds and closes the TLS session.

viz.caption: MAP TYPES FOR DERIVING A NETCONF USERNAME

items.label: Explicit name
items.desc: Username comes from the list entry's auxiliary data.

items.label: Email-style name
items.desc: From the subjectAltName rfc822Name; host part lowercased.

items.label: DNS name
items.desc: From the subjectAltName dNSName, converted to lowercase.

items.label: IP address
items.desc: From the subjectAltName iPAddress, in decimal-dotted quad for IPv4.

items.label: Any of the above
items.desc: First matching rfc822Name, dNSName or iPAddress is used.

items.label: CommonName
items.desc: Converted to UTF-8; use is deprecated.
